utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, ma'am. We are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis this morning presumably for the entire sitting. Judge Stole has something very personal to attend to and will be back with us as soon as possible. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Mitchell. Any preliminaries before we bring in the new witness? All right. Let's finish the documents business relating to yesterday's witness then. Mr. Nikolic? I'm sorry. I see Mr. Thayer. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just wanted to alert the Court that we did not have any objections to any of the documents proffered by any of the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So basically I just need a confirmation that you still wish to tender these documents that are listed in the sheet of paper that was circulated, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. We supplied the list of documents that we are tendering to the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber, and this is the definite list, definitive list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection from any of the other Defence teams? We hear none. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We'd like to tender 1D3310. It is the video clip we showed yesterday to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from any of the other Defence teams? So it is so admitted. All right. Let's proceed with the next witness, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did have one exhibit we wish to tender, and that was P03523, a MUP report type-signed by Mr. Kijac that was used with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you give notice of that to the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't think we distributed the list with that one document, but it was the one document that we did use that was not previously admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay because we are not aware of it. So any objection? Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anyone else who wishes to object? None. So it is also so admitted. Next witness. Any of the documents that have been admitted have been admitted on this condition, namely that if a translation does not exist already, then they will be marked for identification purposes only for the time being pending translation thereof. So that is to be understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grulovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've been summoned as a Defence witness by the accused Beara. Before you give evidence, however, we require from you an undertaking, a solemn undertaking that you will be testifying the truth. The undertaking is formulated in the document that is going to be handed to you now. Please read out that statement aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Grulovic. Please take a seat; make yourself comfortable. Mr. Ostojic is going to put a series of questions to you first. You will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grulovic. As you know, my name is John Ostojic, and I am one of the attorneys who represents Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the record, can you please state your fall name?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: My name is a Branimir Grulovic. My nickname is Bata Grulovic. That's what my friends call me. Should I provide any other personal details? I was born in Belgrade on the 31st of March, 1951. I completed by elementary and high school there, and I went to theatre, TV, drama school in Zagreb, and later on I completed journalist studies -- journalism studies, and I have an MA degree from TV and video production. I am married, and I have four children -- three children. That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grulovic. I'll put some questions to you, sir, and then you'll answer my questions, but thank you for that brief background. So just so the record is clear on the transcript, I note on page 3, line 22, that they are still maintaining yesterday's witness, but I'm sure we can clarify that. Mr. Grulovic, can you share with us a little bit more in detail. You say that you were a journalist or you completed journalistic studies. Can you tell us in your employment history but briefly, we don't want to spend too much time on it, and take us up to and through the year 1995 during the war. In what capacity were you employed and with whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are interested in a particular phase, then you can -- you have our authority to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, let me then restate the question. We'll start -- and we'll get into some of your background because I know it's actually quite interesting having met you, but we are focusing on a specific time period here. Can you tell us from 1991 to 1995 approximately with whom you were employed?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Between 1991 and 1995, I worked in WIS news. That's Reuters TV, and from 1992 until 1997 - that includes the year 1995 - I was the head of the Reuters Balkans office, Reuters TV office for the Balkans. And if we are talking about the Balkans, that's not Balkans in geopolitical terms because -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll clarify that, Mr. Grulovic. I know we are getting a little ahead of ourselves, but I just want to stick with that period that you gave me from 1992 to 1997. You say that you were chief of the -- for Reuters for the Balkan area, but were you not the bureau chief for the section called Balkans from 1992 to 1997? Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. From 1992 until 1997, I was the bureau chief for the Balkan section of the Reuters, and we were headquartered in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Bear with me. Just tell us what a bureau chief means or what your job duties and responsibilities were while you were bureau chief for Reuters.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can safely assume what my duties and responsibilities were, but to put it quite simply I was responsible for all the Reuters TV operations in the area of Croatia, Croatian Krajina, Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, the Republika Srpska, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary, too, so that all the daily news and all the events that occurred in this area were within my jurisdiction. I had to set up teams. I sometimes had to go to the field myself to cover the events and to inform the world public to send the stuff that I did to London.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to speak a little bit slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic -- I leave you, Mr. Ostojic, to explain to him how the system works here and what the problems could be if you overlap and you speak -- or he speaks too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, having been here for a couple of years, I've been advised about myself that I speak too fast. So we've tried to slow it down, and I know that everybody everyone when they take the witness stand can be a tad bit nervous, and please, just relax, and we are going to ask you a couple of questions. As you may realize, there are many people here who are translating and interpreting your words into both B/C/S as well as into English and French, so be patient. If you can look at the screen before you, when you see that the cursor stops, you can proceed with your answer when you hear the full question. Similarly, I'll pay attention to the screen, and I'll try to do the same. So just allow me to put the question to you, and you'll share with us as much information as you know. Would that be acceptable to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do apologise, Your Honours, for speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure it's okay with Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. President. Sir, you tried to mention earlier in your testimony that you when you defined the Balkan, it wasn't the geopolitical sphere of Balkan, and I apologise for having to cut you off, and then I think you touched upon it now. When you were the bureau chief for the Balkans, and we talked about what your responsibilities were as the bureau chief, now tell us how would you describe the territory or area that you covered that has been identified or coined by Reuters as the Balkans wherein you were the bureau chief.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: The area that I covered included those territories in Croatia that were Serb-controlled, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Again, the areas that were controlled by Serbs: Serbia, Montenegro as a state, Albania as a state, Macedonia, Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary. That was the territory that I covered in my reports, and I was responsible for covering the developments there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. A similar question, if I may. What territories did you not cover that one may traditionally feel or think that were -- come under the auspices of the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not cover for security reasons - that was a decision of our central office in London - areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina that were controlled by the Bosniak forces, and in Croatia I did not cover areas that were an integral part of the Republic of Croatia and that were not Serb-controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that would mean, for example, Sarajevo; you did not cover Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I did not cover Sarajevo, but during the war I went to Sarajevo twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if I may with the Court's permission show you 2D547, which is a list of foreign reporters in former Yugoslavia. Just to take a look at it, it's a lengthy document, but I'm going too direct your attention specifically to page 14 of that document, and it should be in e-court, again, under number 2D547. Mr. Grulovic, you let me know when you have that first page of that document in front of you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not the first page that we have on the screen. It's page 14, which I think is just as acceptable. If we can just scroll the paper down to the latter half of that page, and you'll see there, sir, in the caption which is underlined which says "Reuters TV." Do you see that? Do you see that, sir? Mr. Grulovic, are you able to hear me?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see under the Reuters TV section, is your name anywhere on that list?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me see. Yes, I see it. It's listed under 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just generally tell us, who are the other people that follow your name under number 1? Who are these other individuals, in a general sense? Were they assistants, camera men, other journalists, reporters? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I'll take it in order. Dragomir Dragas is listed under 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grulovic. Just generally speaking. I don't need -- I don't really need to know specifically.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, these were all cameramen, producers, but there is a mistake. The name is not Gerald Moser. It's Gerald Williams Moser. That was his middle name. He is listed under 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just a little more -- thank you for that. Just a little more background so we can get a feeling for what you did. You mentioned during your direct -- or during your answers here this morning that you reported to London, correct, to your news bureau in London?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this is during that entire period from 1992 through 1997 while you were bureau chief for Reuters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And share with us, if you will, the day-to-day activities of a bureau chief. What are some of the things that you would do? I mean, you would hunt down a story; you would follow a story; you'd -- what would you do during that time period?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's an interesting question. The daily activities boil down, first of all, to learning what is happening in the field and then analyzing the news coming in, the reports coming in from the field, and then we had to respond professionally, to decide whether to cover an event or not to cover an event. That meant that we had to decide whether would we would send a team to an area, and in many cases I would accompany those teams. I can say that I went there much too often because that's not the usual practice for bureau chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During your time as a bureau chief while being in the Balkan as a Balkan area bureau chief, did you have an opportunity to meet some of the political and military figures that were involved in the war that was going on in Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met some of the persons quite often, both in the military and in the civilian authorities; in other words, politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you -- and I know it's in the news last night and this morning. Did you ever have an opportunity to meet or observe Dr. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, were you able to -- during that tenure from 1992 to 1997 and prior to that time period while you were a news journalist and bureau chief, were you able to assess or determine what the dynamics were between the Serb nationalists and the former JNA officers, former JNA military officers? Were you able to get a feel for what that dynamic was, if any?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I built this feel as time went by; but in brief, I don't think that there was a lot of trust between the politicians and the military figures. Why did I reach this conclusion? Because I often heard some politicians term the army officers "commies," and that's a derogatory term for former members of the JNA because we had all grown up in a socialist system, they as well as I, and it simply did not make the politicians trust those officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, we spoke about having known or met Dr. Karadzic; did you ever have the opportunity and occasion to meet Mr. Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get into those specifics, and thank you for bearing with me. Did you learn at any time whether or not Mr. Beara was a former JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't learn that. I knew that from before because I served in the JNA, and I knew -- or rather, at that time I didn't know Mr. Beara, but I knew that he had been in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, having met and spent significant -- or some time in the Balkans and in Pale and other areas in Bosnia, were you able, sir, to determine or did you ever do a news story in connection with promotions of certain officers who were politically parallel with the ideology of Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Not reports of stories to that effect, but I had an opportunity to talk to people many times, and I came to realize that some officers - don't, please, ask me about their names because I can't recall them; that's a big problem with me; I can't remember names - were ideologically quite close to the policy advocated by Mr. Karadzic. But this policy was a hard-line nationalist policy, which was different to what other officers I knew advocated, including Colonel Beara. Those were people who had been brought up and who genetically were in favour of tolerance and what we called the brotherhood and unit because at one point they had all taken an oath to defend brotherhood and unity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we can try to get a time frame for these sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your answer to my rather broad question that you are not good with names, but sir, you do remember some instances where there were promotions of some officers and demotions of others, such as, let's say, Vasiljevic or Grujic, do you not? Do you have a recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you be a little specific to the best of your recollection as to when that happened, and if you have to break it down, before or after 1992 or 1994, whatever period you want or whatever period you recall, can you give us an indication of when certain officers were demoted, to the best of your recollection, and when others who were parallel ideologues with Mr. Karadzic were, indeed, promoted?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. I was present when there was reshuffle in the command of the 2nd Krajina corps in the command; that's Western Bosnia, the 2nd Krajina corps, and then General Grujic, if I remember correctly, I think that was his name, he was replaced by another officer. And the Chief of Staff in the same corps was also replaced at the same time, General Mica Vlaisavljevic - I hope I remember his name correctly - and another officer was appointed to that post. I think talking about General Mica Vlaisavljevic, since I had an opportunity to have a lengthy conversation with him, I think that he was replaced as a direct consequence of this misunderstanding or conflict that we were speaking about a little while earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's help the Prosecutor here a little bit, although I think he has the information. What period of time was this, sir? Was this before or after 1995, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Before 1995. Let's say that was towards the end of 1994, in the winter of 1994 or maybe the beginning of 1995. I can't tell you precisely, but in any case it was during the winter, and it was either towards the end of it or the beginning -- the beginning of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Grulovic. I don't know that we need any more specificity unless you have it other than that. Now, sir, you mentioned the 2nd Krajina corps. Can you describe for us where that is? I know you said it was in the western part of Bosnia. Could you be more specific by identifying the town or a town that's near that area?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know much about the area of responsibility of the 2nd corps, but when we're talking about towns this was in the area of Petrovac and Drvar and also Grahovo. Those would be the bigger settlements in the area of that corps as far as I can remember. The command of the 2nd Krajina corps was on the mountain pass called Ostrelj between the towns of Petrovac and Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all we needed. I'm not asking you to become a military witness here and tell us what their zone of responsibility may have been but just the Drvar and Petrovac area is adequate for us for this time. Can you tell me, sir, from 1992 and 1995, was there any activity from your prospective as a TV journalist, any activity in that area in the western front of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course there were activities, but 1994 was more interesting for the media because it was the first time when we actually started covering the area when the Bosnian forces launched their offensive from Bihac in the direction of Petrovac, and when this offensive was launched, Mr. Karadzic as the president of Republika Srpska for the first time in one part of the territory of Republika Srpska proclaimed the state of war, which was also very interesting for the media because by then the war had been going on for awhile, and that was the first time when it was actually officially proclaimed as the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, you were there to cover that story, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I was there, and I assume that all the people in this courtroom have seen the footage of Mr. Karadzic wearing a uniform for the first time. This is my own footage, and I interviewed Mr. Karadzic at the time. It is a well known image that has travelled the world several times over.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I haven't asked you about some of your accomplishments yet, sir, but what I would like to do is to -- from my understanding as a journalist you either can break a story, and that would be significant, or as some journalists say, they miss a story, and that's as we say in America "egg on your face." Would those two things basically what journalists consider to be significant?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. We were always in competition with our competitors. Obviously, it was a big professional success if you break a piece of big news. Maybe my previous words sounded a bit like self-promotion, but this was not my intention. I just wanted to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that the footage that I mentioned proves that I was there during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that anybody is going to doubt that, but thank you for that, and we appreciate that. What I'd like to ask you now, sir, before we get into some more specific issues is, just describe for us because there were many journalists there - we've had a couple testify here; we have a few other that may -- will come - just tell -- give us an idea of how accessible it was for news reporters and journalists to come to the Bosnia area to report the developments of the war. Who, if anyone, allowed journalists to gain access to those fronts or those areas?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: The International Press Centre headquartered in Pale had the exclusive right to grant those permissions, and the head of that press centre was Ms. Sonja Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Obviously given -- sorry, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to add that the lady in question is Mr. Karadzic's daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What role to the extent that you know did the military play in allowing or permitting access to news journalists in the Bosnia area during the 1992-1995 period?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: If you wanted to enter Republika Srpska, you did not have to talk to the military. They did not have any rights to issue permits. This was the exclusive purview of the International Press Centre, and the procedure was as follows: You had to submit a written request, you waited for a reply, and when you were given access in a written form, it was only then that you were able to travel to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in 1995, specifically July, sir, do you have a specific recollection as to where you were in the former -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina covering the war? Do you remember the specific place or approximate location?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Not approximately. I can tell you exactly that during that period of time, I was in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps in Petrovac and Drvar. Actually, I was in the command of the 2nd Krajina corps on Mount Ostrelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As we know just from the public records and other indictments that are alleged, there was this operation -- or spring offensive that was being conducted during that time. Do you remember that at all? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the name was. I believe it was offensive summer rather than offensive winter. It is true that I arrived in the area, but the situation was somewhat different from the rest of Republika Srpska. Ms. Karadzic had forbidden me to go to Republika Srpska for some personal reasons of hers. Not only did she stop me but also the Reuters teams and crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll talk about that in a second or two, sir. I'm just trying to get to you a certain place to the best of your recollection. And if we look at it on a timeline, as I think we've agreed and as the news has carried, if you look at the events that start to unfold in Srebrenica when Srebrenica fell, generally speaking, without tying any date that the Prosecution may not wish to agree to, we say approximately on the 11th of July, 1995, Srebrenica fell. Do you remember that date, sir? It's of significance, and you as a news journalist may or may not, but do you remember that date, the day that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: My simple answer would be, yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's try to keep it simple for the time being. Thank you for that, sir. Now, can you tell us where you were on or about the time that you learned that Srebrenica fell in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I can't give you the name of the place, but it was in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps, and the facility was as it was called then a forward command post, but I wouldn't be able to give you the exact name of that location. Don't ask me because I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. You are doing just fine by giving us that you were in the 2nd Krajina corps, and we know that that's in Western Bosnia near Drvar, and we'll get to that in a second. It's a significant -- was it significant for you, sir, for a number of reasons having known that you heard the news from other journalists, your competitors, that Srebrenica fell and you were not there to cover the story or to break the story? Is that also why you have such a recollection as to where you were on that given time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is leading, Mr. Ostojic. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you share with us why you know or how you know and how you can recall that you were in the 2nd Krajina corps during the time that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: The question calls for a bit lengthier answer if you will allow me to provide some more explanation by way of answering the question. First of all, I remember the date because around that time was the time of my summer holiday. My summer holiday was approaching. That's how I know that it was July because according to the work schedule, as soon as I returned to Belgrade I was supposed to take my annual leave. The news on the fall of Srebrenica obviously put my annual leave in question for professional reasons, and I learned about the fall of Srebrenica on the radio. I always carried a small UKT radio with me all the time in order to be able to listen to the world news. The communications at the time were not what they are today, and very often that small radio was my only way of communicating with the world. Obviously, for professional reasons I wanted to be able to confirm that piece of news from the sources close to the Republika Srpska army, and given my personal acquaintance and -- with and the presence of Colonel Beara, I obviously approached him, asking him whether he could either confirm or deny the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Grulovic, we are going to get into that a little bit later. I'm just trying to at least now get an idea of where you were at that significant moment in history, and we'll get into that specifically. Thank you for reminding me. Sir, what I'd like to know is just from practical standpoint. Here you are, a newsman on the western front, and on the opposite side by the Drina river where Srebrenica enclave is, there's a significant news story occurring. Did you go directly from the 2nd Krajina corps area to Srebrenica with your team in order to cover the Srebrenica story, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, where did you go. This is leading on this topic. I think we should go traditionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You know, I could ask him that. Obviously he has heard the question, Mr. President. I think -- it's incorrect. I mean, if you look at the question, we are certainly -- he's -- I could ask it if he wants in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, where, if anywhere, did you go from the 2nd Krajina corps after you learned that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously, I headed for Belgrade, and I have to explain how I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question so that we don't have any more --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. My answer would be I headed for Belgrade then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grulovic, for being patient with me. Why didn't you go directly to Srebrenica from the 2nd Krajina corps? Why did you go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: The reason was simple. The press centre had never allowed me to go to Western Bosnia and be in the zone of the 2nd Krajina corps, so if I had turned up there, I would have put myself at risk of being arrested, even.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So let's just walk through this before we get to your discussion with Mr. Beara in the 2nd Krajina corps at the time that Srebrenica fell. You leave from the 2nd Krajina corps to go to Belgrade so that you can do what, if anything, sir? Because you mentioned the holiday there. Were you trying to regain access into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I have to explain how I had arrived in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why don't you do that. How did you arrive to the 2nd Krajina corps in the first place?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, there was already a ban on me entering the territory of Republika Srpska, and the ban was issued by the International Press Centre. I insisted on a permit, but every time I did the response was negative. They would always deny me access, and I even received information that my name was made known at all the border crossings and that there was a strict ban on my entering the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you share with us who implemented or imposed this strict ban on you, and I presume, but you can tell us, was that a ban on Reuters as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The measure was imposed by the International Press Centre, or rather, Ms. Sonja Karadzic as the head of the press centre; and the ban did not apply only to me personally but unfortunately to all the crews, all the Reuters crews that were based and working from Belgrade. And as for the local Reuters team members that were working from Pale, their movements were also restricted pursuant to the order of the International Press Centre, i.e., Ms. Sonja Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, just so I'm understanding you, you then were in that sense a news -- TV news reporter who was in the former Bosnia without proper credentialed authorisation from Ms. Sonja Karadzic, and therefore at that time you returned to Belgrade, correct, during the time that Srebrenica had fallen? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just so I have a better appreciation for what you do, do you, sir, have local support staff who assist you in various parts of different areas, such as the western and eastern areas of a republic or state?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had teams in Pale, and I had teams in Banja Luka and certain towns, and I had a team in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As a bureau chief, sir, you would over the course in the years in having been a journalist, you would develop these contacts and you would maintain those contacts and use them when the need arose depending on where the news story was breaking. Is that the way it essentially worked?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. You have to have contacts. You can't function in professional terms without any contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So now, just take us briefly when you were in Belgrade and after the fall of Srebrenica; what if anything did you do? Did you go on this holiday, or did you try to gain access to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I tried to gain access to Srebrenica, but there was no chance in hell for me to get credentials from the International Press Centre. I was turned down, in no uncertain terms, very rudely. I spoke to Ms. Karadzic personally over the phone, and she was very rude, bad-mannered, using certain words and terms not really becoming of a lady. And in my desperation to have to talk to a person like that, a person who was in a high position, I sent a letter to the Chief of Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and to Mr. Karadzic, the president of Republika Srpska to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to Mr. Krajisnik, the speaker of the parliament, asking them to allow them to perform my duties professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, can you give us an idea to the extent that you know or were ever told, did Ms. Karadzic, Sonja Karadzic, restrict and forbid you access to Bosnia because you were an objective journalist, or did she restrict it because you were providing news stories in favour of the Serbs, or do you know if at all how -- why it was restriction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The last part of the question is, if you know, why do you think she forbade you, but the other parts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to move it along. I'll ask it in the general sense, and I can appreciate his comment on that. So if I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In any case, he has heard the question now --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and whichever way you rephrase it, I think he knows what the sort of question he is expected to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn, Mr. Grulovic, or have an appreciation as to why Sonja Karadzic restricted Reuters and yourself from covering news during this 1992-through-1995 period?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sonja told me that personally in that telephone conversation. Allegedly, it was because of my very close ties with the Army of Republika Srpska, allegedly, and she also mentioned some other reasons which are of no relevance whatsoever for my testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, can you share with us whether there were any restrictions by the various military or, as you say, the army of you reporting anything that you wanted to? Did they tell you you can report certain things and you couldn't report others? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, the answer would be there were no restrictions whatsoever or hindrances on behalf of any member of the Republika Srpska army. I did not experience any such things either personally or any member of my crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a general question; then we'll try to get to some of the more specific issues that I'd like to address with you. At any time during this period, and specifically in 1994 and 1995, were you, sir, ever criticized by Serbs for relaying too much information or not -- tainting the story in the favour of the Serbs or not? Were you ever criticized or any criticisms asserted against you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that I published a lot of stories which were then portrayed as anti-Serbian. However, my excuse was the fact that I am familiar and I was familiar with the mentality of these people because I belonged to that people myself, that they never showed any anger towards such stories if they thought that they were truthful. They would always react if the truth was distorted or being manipulated, so I could use the fact that I was familiar with the mentality of my -- of the members of my ethnic group, and I published things as they were. They would criticize me sometimes using swear words, which was part of our folklore, but then they would say -- they would add to that, but everything is just as you published it, and that was the long and the short of the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Now, let me ask you about Mr. Beara. You had mentioned during this morning's portion of your testimony that you have known him and you know him. Can you share with us how long you have known Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Beara by pure chance at the very beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and during the war I saw him on several occasions. I mostly saw him far from where military operations were actually taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'm not sure if you've completed your answer. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be the essence of my answer. I don't think that there is any need for me to elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure, thank you for that. Now, sir, you also mentioned specifically Mr. Beara, having seen him when you heard the news that Srebrenica fell. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's not what he said, and that's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have a recollection of seeing Mr. Beara at all immediately prior to the time that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I've already said that. I said it at the beginning of my testimony. I saw him in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's okay. We'll cover it again, and I thought you did as well. Can you tell me, sir, did you see him face to face?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. How else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you, sir, at that time speak to him at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Bear with us to the best of your recollection that conversation that you had with Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: If we're to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get some kind of time frame. There's a lot of time before Srebrenica fell. I mean, are we talking 1994, 1993? I mean, let's get to some time frames here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think Mr. McCloskey certainly knows given my proofing notes, but I think that he can't quite frankly have his cake and eat it too. If he doesn't allow me to lead, I will go more specific with it, and I think the witness in his prior two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's not make a mountain out of a mole hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'll ask him directly that. We'll put a specific time frame on it, and I don't mind that at all. In fact, I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a serious issue regarding the proofing note and the lack of information, and there's nothing about this in the proofing note. So we can get into this in greater detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't intend to stir up a whole argument on this. Just put your question within the framework, a time framework, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I think we can all agree that Srebrenica fell on July 11th, 1995. Do you recall seeing Mr. Beara on or about that date when you learned that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. I've already answered this question. At the time when Srebrenica fell, I saw Mr. Beara and I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just tell us where you were when you saw and spoke to Mr. Beara at the time that Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've replied already, but let me repeat. In the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps, that would be Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us the contents of that specific conversation that we are talking about, which was the day that Srebrenica fell where you saw Mr. Beara face to face and had this conversation? Can you share with us to the best of your recollection what was said by you and from Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I think I can. It was approximately at the time when I learned about the fall of Srebrenica. Naturally, I immediately sought to confirm the news, and I used the fact that I knew Colonel Beara, and I asked him if he could confirm or deny that or if he could provide some more information, and his response was quite short. He said, I myself don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what did you do after that, sir, if anything?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to call my house in Belgrade over the phone. I had some difficulties, and then I decided to return to Belgrade as soon as possible and to launch the proceedings to obtain permission to go to that part of the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And as you told us, you left that 2nd Krajina Corps to go to Belgrade. How did you go -- how did you leave, by bus, by car, by helicopter? What means of transportation did you utilize to go from the 2nd Krajina Corps to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to answer that question I would first have to tell you how I managed to get into the area of the 2nd Krajina corps. Since there was this ban, I was prohibited from entering Republika Srpska. This ban was put in place by Ms. Karadzic, the international bureau at Pale, in other words; and since there were interesting things going on from the media point of view - I talking about the summer offensive - I sought assistance from the Army of Republika Srpska, and the Army of Republika Srpska sent a military jeep with two military police officers to Belgrade, and they smuggled me across the border, quite literally, and took me to the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps. And I spent some time there, with their blessing, and I also have to say with some degree of protection that they accorded me. And I went back to Belgrade in the same way again, a military jeep and two military police officers who again smuggled me across the border and took me back to Belgrade. It is not difficult to assume that -- or to guess that this was organised by the army with the blessing of all those officers who might be responsibile for such an operation. First of all, I'm talking about the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever, sir, obtain access to go to the Srebrenica enclave or in that area to cover any of the news that was unfolding at that time, July of 1995, subsequent, of course, to the fall of the 11th of July, 1995, and that's the time period I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not get the permission, but many days later - now I can't recall the date, but it was perhaps late July, early August - a Reuters team from Pale was granted permission to go to the Srebrenica area. But I remember quite well that this was not what we had expected, in professional terms, and this leads one to conclude that they did not get permission to move about freely unlike some other teams that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now -- and we'll get back to this meeting or the time that you saw Mr. Beara at the date that Srebrenica fell in a little bit, but let me ask you this: Prior to July of 1995, you had an occasion, as you told us, to meet Mr. Beara. Did you ever have an occasion to assist him in making any telephone calls or using the Reuters satellite phones?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was again in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps, which is where I was with my teams. We were fully equipped, and we had satellite phones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you -- to the best of your recollection, do you recall whether or not Mr. Beara at any time requested to use the Reuters satellite phone for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beara did not ask for that, but I offered to him this opportunity to call his family because I knew that he and many others whose families were far away had not seen them for a long time, and it was impossible to establish contact if one didn't have a satellite phone. Colonel Beara then called his mother. At that time, she was living in Split in Croatia. I was present during this conversation. What really impressed me and I was touched, I was moved emotionally, was the fact that Colonel Beara called his mother "Nona." It's a typical word from the Dalmatian dialect, and he asked about her health, her security situation, too, knowing that the Croats knew full well where he was, and yet his mother was there in Split. It was also my impression -- well, we didn't speak after that conversation, but it was my impression that Colonel Beara was quite sure that no one would harm his mother, which was quite surprising for me because I knew all about the relations between Serbs and Croats. This conversation between Colonel Beara and his mother lasted for a short time, but in terms of emotions and the emotional messages that were exchanged, I think it had great significance both for Colonel Beara and for his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for sharing that with us, sir. Do you recall any other instance in which Mr. Beara at -- either you allowing him to or inviting him to use the Reuters satellite phone sometime after this phone conversation with his mother in Split but before the fall of Srebrenica, that time period so we don't go too broad, do you remember that he utilized the phone at any other time, in your presence, of course?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember this, but it was not Colonel Beara who used the phone. He was present there when I offered a young officer of the Republika Srpska army to use the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you help us to narrow the date down? Do you know when it was? And not specifically the -- necessarily the day, but if you could give us a month or a year, to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are striking events, and it is much more -- much easier to remember them. That was in the spring and the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, this officer or this person, this young officer that you allowed in the presence of Mr. Beara to use the Reuters satellite phone, do you remember, sir, what his ethnic background was or his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. He was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Could you remember, sir, if at all, his name or his nickname?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall his name, but his nickname was Kikan.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I could help you with that. In looking at some of -- please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Kikan is probably a nickname based on his last name, which might have been Kikanovic, then but I can't recall his first name, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In some of the documents that the Prosecution has provided to us from time to time, and I'll read if I may be permitted to lead on this to see if I can refresh the witness's recollection. We have in some of the documents, and that's Exhibit 2D546, a name on page 24 of a gentleman called Eldar Kikanovic. Does that ring a bell to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Eldar. It's a strange name. One would think I would remember it, but no, but his last name was Kikanovic. He was a Bosniak, and it's quite possible that his first name was Eldar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can you share with us to the best of your recollection that telephone call that this young officer called Kikan made. Do you remember to whom he made it and what was said during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it's much easier to remember those emotionally charged things than perhaps some others. In our presence, Kikan called his parents. They lived in Tuzla at the time. I remember that his mother picked up the phone, and his mother couldn't believe that she was really talking to her son because she had received information that he had been killed, and he tried to convince her that he was really her son. His mother refused to talk to him, persistently, and then she handed the phone to his father, and then he told his father various details from his childhood to convince him that it really was he. After awhile, I can't remember how long it took, the father finally was convinced that he was speaking to his son, and it was very, very moving. All of us present there were moved, and I noticed that Colonel Beara was crying. All of us who were in the room, well, we were all very moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Sir, I'd like if we can talk a little bit about -- a little more about Mr. Beara, and you shared with us some of the times that you visited or met with him and the observations that you made. Can you tell us whether or not you have formulated some sort of assessment or -- about the kind of person that Mr. Beara was? Were you able to do that or glean that from the meetings and the times that you met with him? Describe for us what type of person he was.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: My impression of Colonel Beara is based to a certain extent with sports. First of all, I found it easy to remember his name because his last name is the same as that of Vladimir Beara. He was a famous goalkeeper. He was my idol in sports, and at our first meeting, in fact, this is what we discussed, whether the two were related, and I would have been very happy to be able to say that I had met a relative of my sports idol. The next thing that really impressed me was his Dalmatian dialect. It was always very pleasant on the ear, at least as far as I was concerned. Secondly, his voice, kind of bossa -- baritone. This is something that also left an impression on me. But the voice, the penetrating stare, and the firm hand grip, I went beyond that; and in talking to him, I also realized that there was some kind of gentleness there, too, and I was able to see this in the informal conversations when we talked about our children, my children, his children, my family, his family, the plans, what we wanted, our wishes as men, as parents, as fathers. So my impression of Colonel Beara is -- I'm not going to budge from there. He is a kind person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you for that. Now, Mr. Grulovic, I want to just ask a little bit more about your background information. After 1997 when you ceased being the Balkan chief for Reuters, what if anything did you do? Did you work for any other organisation or entity?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: For a year and a half, I worked for the Austrian state television, ORF, and at that time the Austrian ambassador and the international coordinator for Kosovo was Ambassador Wolfgang Petritsch, and since I worked for the Austrian TV, I was in frequent contact with him. At first, those were official contacts, and later on we also had private contacts, and when Mr. Petric was appointed a high representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, the OHR, I was invited to become a media advisor, and I accepted this offer, and I was there in 2000 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And after subsequent to that, sir, were you gainfully employed or --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to continue. For a year after the change of the regime in Belgrade, I was appointed the director general of the city TV channel in Belgrade, TVB, and after a year I decided not to be professionally engaged in TV actively. I switched to theory, and I got my MA degree, and now I teach media studies in Banja Luka and Novi Sad as an associate lecturer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and sir, I just want to go through some documents that I was hoping to go through with you. Earlier at the beginning of your direct examination, we talked a little bit about the dynamics, if you will, of the civilian pro- nationalists and their relationships or feelings towards the former JNA officers. Did you, sir, make an assessment as to whether or not that was only on a level at, let's say, the Presidency or a higher level, or did you also gain an appreciation, if that was true, at other levels, such as at the local level?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I like to say that those were crazy times, and I think they really were. Of course, at grass-root level among the people there were those who were for and those who were against, but if we are talking about those lower levels, especially if we are talking about the ordinary people, they were not preoccupied with politics. What they were really concerned with is how to make a living, how to survive, how to keep what can be kept, and that is why I am -- I believe that this was generated from a centre and then disseminated through propaganda activities, and some people bought into this propaganda, but most of the ordinary people did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, as a TV news journalist, I understand that you obviously put yourself and your staff at risk in order to allow the rest of the world to see things as they have developed in a certain area. Can you share with me if you were ever, aside from -- well, can you share with me if you will if you were ever threatened or felt at ease at any instance during the coverage of the war, and try to be as specific as possible as to when that time period was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure the gentleman had several threats as he covered this war, but I don't see how this is relevant to our case and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There was an instance, actually, from my understanding in meeting with the witness that Mr. Beara was present during one incident in which he -- or at least I -- he felt that he was threatened, and I wanted to draw that out from him. It's certainly relevant, I believe, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But apart from Beara's alleged presence, how does that round up relevancy-wise?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It actually defines further how Mr. Beara is, I think and I think this witness having had those contacts with him. If the Court feels -- I can move on. It isn't as significant to me particularly, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the first time I heard of Beara's presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, it may lend some relevance to him, but if he can point out to me in the proofing note or the -- anything else, but I still ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't catch the last part of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you alleging that Beara, your client, did something on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll make it easy for the Prosecutor. I'll just withdraw that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- and I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, thank you very much for your time, and the other counsel here are going to have an opportunity to ask you questions as will my learned friend from the Prosecution and possibly the Court. We appreciate it very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we will have a break now. We can ask afterwards as well. We can do it now. Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a cross-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll have some questions, Your Honour. It would take less than half an hour, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have -- and Mr. Haynes, I take it you don't have any questions, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the transcript, line 11. I'm supposed to have said Mr. Sarapa. I never mentioned Mr. Sarapa. I asked Mr. Krgovic, and we don't have Mr. Krgovic there. We have Mr. Sarapa instead. That should be corrected, and the first part of his answer is missing too. He said that he has got a few questions. All right. Do you agree we have a break now? 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grulovic. My name is a Dragan Krgovic, and on behalf of General Gvero's Defence team I'm going to ask you several questions related to your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Since the two of us are speaking the same language - Serbian, that is - I would kindly ask you to make a short break after the end of my question in order to allow the interpreters to interpret that question and in order to avoid overlapping. As far as I could understand your testimony, in July 1995 and beginning of August you were not in the territory of Republika Srpska; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: In the second half of July and August, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this was precisely because you had not been given credentials from the International Press Centre and Sonja Karadzic to enter the Republika Srpska as you have explained to my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The time I was there illegally as far as the International Press Centre was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, I'm going to show you a document that I have come across. This is a Document P3540. I'm going to explain. This is a document which is an intercept, which was provided by the security service of the BiH Army, and the date is 5 August 1995, this intercept with a caveat that some family names are misspelled. I'm drawing your attention to the first page, and I would kindly ask you to read --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Can the text be blown up a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have a hard copy for you, sir, so I would kindly ask the usher to provide the hard copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a conversation between a Colonel Stevanovic, but I believe that the last name has either been misspelled or the person was not a member of the Main Staff, and a certain woman by the name of Sonja, and it concerns your request to be present in the territory Republika Srpska and reporting from there. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this paragraph starts with the words "Can you help me with something." Somewhere in the middle of the page, the second paragraph. "Reuters, you know, Bata Grulovic." That's how it starts. He is blocked in Belgrade. Could we possibly issue him with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, page 2 in English. I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a bit of a lengthy intercept. Before asking him questions, could we give him a chance to read through it, especially since his name is on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is going to be, but -- what is the question going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to show the intercept to the witness in order to show him that this is about his attempts to enter the territory Republika Srpska and to have him confirm what he remembers from the period. That would be my line of questioning with regard to this document, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Then Witness, Mr. Grulovic, please take your time and have a look at the document and read it out before you will answer any further questions. You have a hard copy of it in front of you, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've already read the document that I've been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also have a look at the second page of the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please do that, and could you please pay attention to paragraph in the middle of the page which starts with the words -- the small part which starts with the word "Listen, we can convey your message." Page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's a good idea that the witness take some time to read the entire document before answering questions about it. It will just save misunderstandings, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I suggested to the witness, but I think he understood me to say that I was referring to page 1. I'm referring to the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also please look at the third page, Mr. Grulovic, or at least a part thereof. Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it seems that this intercept confirms what you have told us and that was the -- that the International Press Centre had a total media control over the territory, and this International Press Centre was headed by Sonja Karadzic, and would you agree with that answer?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And every journalist who wanted to enter Republika Srpska and to report from there had to have that centre's approval; there was no other body authorised to issue such an approval according to what you remember. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this applied to all journalists, not only to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: The way I have already explained the principle was this: You had to submit a request to the International Press Centre to enter Republika Srpska, and it was very exclusive right to either approve the request or deny it. There was nobody else who could do it instead of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And I would like to draw your attention to page 3 in this document, which is an intercept as we have already said. This is the last page in the English version. It says that everybody has to go through us with our authority, and this applies to foreign states. This means that the press centre received authority from the president of the state, which was Radovan Karadzic, and he was the only one who dealt with those matters.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that that's correct. I'm really not familiar with the organisation. I never took any particular interest in it, but only a gullible person could believe that things were different given the fact that it was Mr. Karadzic's daughter who was the head of that press centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, both of you, please. Both Mr. Grulovic and Mr. Krgovic, please slow down. We who are following in English can sense the stress that you are causing amongst the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I apologise, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grulovic, could you please look at the first page of this document and see the way they think about you. I believe that this Sonja is Sonja Karadzic from the press centre and that she speaks about you, and she says, Their intentions are not honest. I believe that this refers to you. Was this Ms. Sonja Karadzic's position towards you and she stated that in no uncertain terms in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll withdraw it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, can you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that I had a personal conflict with Ms. Karadzic concerning honesty and professionalism, but I soon gave up because I had realized that all conversations with her were beside the point and that all my words fell on deaf ears, and I left her the freedom to draw any conclusions she wanted about my possible intentions. Whether these intentions were honest and honourable doesn't really matter. What mattered was whether I was a professional or not, and if I was a professional, then obviously I had to have certain professional integrity. It just went without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, in the second half of July 1996, who did you engage and who worked for Reuters television? Who reported from the zones of responsibility from the 1st and 2nd Krajina corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, already I hired two individuals who were employed with the press bureau of the 2nd Krajina Corps. Their names were Milorad Zoric and Slavisa Sabljic. I equipped them with technical equipment. I provided them with a camera and everything else that was necessary, which also included a vehicle. I could do that only with the consent of the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they reported on your behalf in July and August 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, from November 1994 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you satisfied with the quality of their work or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Slavisa Sabljic was a very experienced journalist, albeit he had gained all that experience working in the printed media and on the radio. Anyway, he did not find it very difficult to shift to television work very quickly after having received some advice. Mr. Zoric is a dissectologist by profession, very well versed in arts, so he was not a stranger to the work with the camera in order to get a good picture. So it was very easy to explain to him how to technically use the equipment that I had provided them with, and I was very happy with the quality of their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How professional and how objective were their reports from the field?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to try and say to the Trial Chamber that they would not have worked for me had I -- had they not been professional in their work, which means I was very happy with the objectivity of their work and the assessments that they made on certain events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Good morning, everyone. Sir, my name is Peter McCloskey. I represent the Office of the Prosecution, and I'll be asking you a few questions, not too many, I hope. Let me stay with this intercept a bit, and I hope you've had a chance to look at it because I want you to take a look at what is being said here, and I think if you look at it carefully you might agree with me what's going on here. First of all, did you know a Lieutenant-Colonel Stevanovic, or have you ever heard of anybody like that from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's the position of the Prosecution that this intercept is a phone call from Sonja Karadzic, the person from the International Press Centre, and it's actually to the VRS Main Staff to a -- and they are speaking to someone named Lieutenant-Colonel Stevanovic from the Main Staff, and that looking at the -- it's the 12th line down. They -- it appears that the intercept people got their letters slightly mixed up in the Prosecution's view and that it is Sonja Karadzic that says the following: "You can help me with something." So she is calling the VRS main staff, and she says, "You can help me with something. Trusting the female soul, I hope that we will get this job done. Now, this is what it's about, disregarding that you have an adverse point of view, you know, I will try to ask you something so we get something done together. Now, this is what it's about. Reuters, you know, Bata Grulovic is blocked in Belgrade. Can you make it possible that we issue for him, you know, and that he passes with it, but I have been here for five or six days. Before that, I was up there with Talic, and I don't want to go on like this. I want to go through you." So she doesn't want to go through Talic. She wants to go through this guy at the Main Staff. This is clearly a female because she's saying "trusting the female soul." I don't know about you, but when a woman says "trusting the female soul" she's trying to get something, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we ask the peanut gallery to knock off the noise? It's repeated, and everyone can hear it, and the groaning is just not appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In any event, she says "trusting the female soul," and then she goes on to say that you're blocked in Belgrade and that she wants you to issue a -- wants these guys to issue a pass. So then keep looking down it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish the question, and then I will give you an opportunity, of course. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We look down it, and X, who I can suggest to you is this Main Staff lieutenant-colonel, says, "You know that there's a strict order from the president of the country that permits are issued only by the International Press Centre." And then in our view, we go down and you can read what it says, and then S, which I believe is Sonja, says, "We have the collective opinion that it should be provided to him. Now they complain they would like to send, you know, pictures up there, et cetera." And then X, who I think is this lieutenant-colonel from the Main Staff, says, "Let me ask you something. How much do you know about Reuters and Bata Grulovic and their people and editors politics?" And then Sonja says, "Most likely less than you, but I have the impression that their intentions are honest and that" -- and then this is the Main Staff colonel that says, see, "Trust me.
