They don't have honest intentions." And then they go around and, you know, you've seen this. They say a lot of bad things about you and that -- about your ego and other things. So if you look at it in that perspective, it appears you've misread Sonja Karadzic and that it's really the VRS Main Staff that are the ones controlling the permits and have not allowed you to go to the RS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you still wish to raise an objection? Mr. Josse first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. It's an outrageous question. It's a comment. It isn't really a question at all. It's a submission. How can the witness seriously deal with it? And it's completely improper, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I join that, Mr. President, but also, it mischaracterizes what's on the face of the document, also, with absolutely no basis for the Prosecution to say that he suggests there's this mistake or a change of the letters. If you look at the beginning part of it, it's rather clear, and I think -- I also join but -- and I stress that it is -- it does call for speculation on this witness's part, and hopefully he will have other evidence on it, but it is just comment by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's interesting we've switched hats on these intercepts for a moment, but they in their question concluded that the people that were being critical of this man were the -- was Sonja and the International Press Centre, and anybody's reading of this sees that that's just not right, and that's what I'm asking him about. He is in a position to look at this and tell us, and am I going to get double-teamed by these guys? It's not a problem, but I think Mr. Krgovic should be able to speak for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Stop, stop. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One last point, and thank you, Mr. President, just to reply. We obviously led the witness. We didn't identify this document nor let it -- the witness has testified about a personal conversation he had and his impressions that he gleaned from Ms. Sonja Karadzic, and this intercept, he can ask him if he wants based on that, but this witness specifically had personal contacts and telephone conversations with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, all right, all right. Come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that the peanut gallery?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, for the future let's start from here. Once this witness was cross-examined by Mr. Krgovic, please restrict yourself to the practice that we have adopted so far. I needn't say more. As of course the question itself, we think it's a very fair question considering the witness's previous conclusion deriving from the content of this intercept which he read. So we are authorizing the question, and we are asking the witness to answer it. Have you understood the question, Mr. Grulovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then could you perhaps tell us whether your previous answer was right or wrong or whether you could have been wrong in your assessment that was it was Ms. Karadzic that was mounting an opposition rather than the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honours, I will have to be a little bit rude, and I do apologise to all the ladies present in the courtroom. Mr. Prosecutor does not know Ms. Karadzic. If he knew her, he would know that she doesn't have a soul, least of all a female soul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it lightly for one moment because Ms. Karadzic is not here to defend herself. Let's moderate ourselves and how we attack other people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't want to moderate my views, and I'm ready to answer any legal suits that Ms. Karadzic may decide to file against me. But I state that it was Sonja Karadzic that prevented me to operate professionally in Republika Srpska, and I confirm that I had excellent cooperation with the Army of Republika Srpska, with most of the high-ranking officers in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You've got your answer, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to a document that is 65 ter 3538. Sir, you read English, I take it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I would prefer to have a document in the Serbian language in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. There should be a translation. If we do have that, we'll be able to give that to you. You had testified that you wrote your articles and you wrote them truthfully and sometimes Serbs didn't like that and they complained to you about it, but they never said that you weren't writing about the truth. And so let me ask you about -- I've got a -- what is a Reuters article on the Factiva Net that is dated 11 January 1996. Again, take your time to read it. Really about Serbs fleeing Sarajevo and settling in the ruins of the former Muslim village, northeast Bosnia, which the Serb artillery destroyed in 1993; that's the first line. I want to call your attention down to -- I think it's the sixth paragraph, and it appears you have said, "Konjevic Polje has been a virtual ghost town since its Muslim population was driven out by the Bosnian Serb army, little more than a traffic control post on the road between Belgrade and Sarajevo. It straggles along the floor of a mountain valley on the Bosnian Serb bank of the Drina border with RUMP Yugoslavia. The Bosnian Serb army ethnically cleansed all Muslims from Eastern Bosnia during the fighting." Then, "Konjevic Polje is only a few miles north of Srebrenica where some 4.000 unarmed Muslim prisoners of war were allegedly massacred by the BSA after the town's capture last July. Muslim escapees were killed in the woods around Konjevic Polje as they tried to flee the Srebrenica massacre and find safely in Muslim-held territory around Tuzla to the west." Do you stand by that article?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, this is not an article that I wrote. Secondly, if you knew how journalism operates, you would realise this is a text that was published in the printed press, not on TV. It was not broadcast on TV, so I'm not the author of this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it says by Brata Grulovic. Do you know any other Brata Grulovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a byline, and you could put anyone's name here. I claim here and I'm ready to face any consequence of this claim that this is not my text, and I openly express my suspicion that this is a forgery. All the texts exist in the Reuters files. You can talk to them, and perhaps then you would get the original text. I also would like to express my suspicion that on the 11th of January, 1996, I was not in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it possible this information went out over the Reuters wire service and your name is on it just because you were the chief?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I did not report for editorials, or rather, the text. I did my reports for TV. This is not a TV text. The TV reports in the written form must contain the date, source, shortlist, all the other elements that pertain to TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the substance of this, do you disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to discuss an article that I doubt I wrote at all. Konjevic Polje in 1996, an editorial text, I don't recall ever having done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you -- one moment. Do you still wish to intervene, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the questions are going to persist, the objection would be it calls for a legal conclusion, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see. What's your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was whether he agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. He's answered that question. Your next question? I think he has answered the question. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, he said he would not answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said he doesn't want to discuss an article about which he has got --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's disregard that this says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's disregard this printout says it's from Reuters and that it's got your name on it. Just by itself, this comment that the Muslim population was driven out by the Bosnian-Serb army, do you agree with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really can't agree with something that I didn't write. If I have to comment what some unidentified author has written, then I don't think that this is a proper question. Please give me the name of the author of a text that has been published, and then I can read it and I can analyse it. But if it is now being imputed to me that I wrote this and I didn't, now I have to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. Now, we were patient before because we respected the position that you took that this article was being wrongly attributed to you when you deny paternity completely, but now the question is different. No one is suggesting to you that irrespective of what you said it's still being attributed to you. Granted for argument sake that this is, as you say, not an article written by you; that's notwithstanding, having had a look at it, you are being asked to state whether you agree with its contents or not, and your answer should be based on your personal knowledge of the events and independently of the authorship of this article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in Srebrenica during the events in Srebrenica and around it. I can only agree with the fact that every town that has been destroyed, every village that has been burnt, that has been abandoned, where nobody lives regardless of their ethnic background or religion looks like a ghost town. I also don't know how many people lived in Konjevic Polje before the war, what the ethnic composition of the population was, so I cannot know and I cannot claim that 4.000 people had been expelled from that area. But whoever was expelled, regardless of what location, regardless of who did it, it is a horrible act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to ask you about another article. This is 65 ter number 3539, and hopefully you'll get it in your language. This is dated 18 November 1996, and I should call it maybe a computer printout as opposed to an article. It's similar computer printout entitled "Reuters," and it says "by Branimir Grulovic." It's dated 18 November 1996, and it's on the topic of the ousted Bosnian-Serb generals, I'm sure a topic that you are familiar with related to Ms. Plavsic and others during that time frame. If you could take a little while to look at this printout. Is this something that you -- this printout from the Reuters -- well, headed by Reuters, is this something that you recall being involved in, getting out -- this information out to the public?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this. I was present there when this meeting took place in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you write this article, or did it go out under your byline?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I have to note, this is not byline. This is information. This is -- these are captions that follow the images because you have to provide some text, too, and this was probably taken out of that, but this was never published as a printed text in the printed media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. This is a wire service, so this information goes out to newspapers and publications all over the world, and they pick it up and then cite Reuters or the AP or something like that, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So unlike the last one we looked at, you can stand by this one to say this was information that you and Reuters sent out on the wire service?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're not sure?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I did send information about these events, but I don't know whether it was in this form or not, but that's not at issue here, so I don't have any objections to this one, unlike for the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. In the second line you say, "top generals except for Mladic and his closest aid General Milan Gvero."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this line of questions, first of all because it is outside of the temporal and territorial frame of the indictment. It's 1996. I don't know what's the is point of this whole line of cross-examination. What is my learned colleague trying to prove here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Reuters articles themselves or the -- whatever we want to call them are particularly relevant. We found one that he is disavowed on the particular events. Now we have found one is he is avowing. We, also, if you recall, had a discussion by this witness of the JNA officers and the effect of the politicians and the nationalist on them. A very broad topic here is a JNA officer, General Gvero, talking about politicians. It's right on point in responding to Mr. Ostojic's cross-examination, and this is -- sorry, direct examination, and this is cross-examination. This is an area I think the Court would want to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Go ahead. Let's hear the whole question. Until now, it appears to us to be quite relevant. If at the end it proves to be the contrary, we'll stop Mr. McCloskey. But otherwise, please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you talked about nationalist politicians, were -- do you put Ms. Plavsic in that group?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only Reuters but the other media characterized Ms. Plavsic as a hard-liner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you note here that Milan Gvero is General Mladic's closest aid. How did you conclude -- come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: General Milan Gvero, as the other generals who were in the Main Staff, are all closest associates of the chief of the Main Staff. They all had their different purviews, so General Milan Gvero as a member of the Main Staff was definitely an associate of the chief of the Main Staff. That's in accordance with the military rules of service, so I still maintain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What this says is he is the closest aid. You can only be one closest in both language. You can't all be the closest. So are you backing off this article in that respect, or are you saying Gvero was Mladic's number-one man?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to take any stance from the written word, but what I'm saying is that General Gvero, like all the other generals, members of the Main Staff, were all very close associates, and each of them had respective purviews. And if we are talking about General Milan Gvero, whether he was the closest assistant to General Mladic, based on this text as I sit here today I have to distance myself from this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you are distancing yourself now as you sit here today. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Because of your remark. You were insisting on him being the closest assistant. I really can't know that, but at the moment when I was drafting this text, I suppose that this is how things were presented to us, and that's where I drew my conclusion from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you think something has changed since the time that you wrote the article? Have you learned something else, or is it because you are testifying and it's hard to testify against your fellows?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just object to the form of the question. I don't know, and I think it's inappropriate for Mr. McCloskey to call him his fellows. He didn't lay a foundation. These are certainly not his fellows. Mr. Grulovic was not in the military at any time, but I object to just that last characterization.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Let's proceed. I think the question is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought he said he was in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, exactly, and what's being suggested to the witness is whether he is biased or not, I mean, and I think he can perfectly answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I think it's a fair question. You've just got to examine your own thoughts and feelings on that.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not biased. I don't have any mental or emotional problems. I can testify against anybody that I deem to deserve something either positive or negative, and I'm saying it again to you, Mr. Prosecutor. Everybody who is sitting close to somebody who is a chief of a military body is their close -- or closest associates as long as they are both sitting in the same body. We could not attend any meetings, which is only natural, and thus we could not draw our own personal conclusion as to who the closest associate of General Mladic's were, whether they were merely close or the closest. However, based on the way things were presented to us, by the sources that we respected, one could arrive at this kind of conclusion. Nothing has changed in the meantime. However, if I were put in the same situation today, I suppose that my sentence would have been drafted in a different way, in a more precise way. It would read better. So we would not have to discuss that sentence as we are doing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to interview General Gvero at any time during or after the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to emphasize that those were not interviews. Those were statements for the media, press statements, and then based on those statements, you know how the mechanism works. You were allowed to maybe put in a question edgewise, but I wouldn't say that this was the true form of an interview as part of the journalist profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was it that you were able to ask General Gvero questions?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I know that we had several official encounters during which we could talk to him. He provided his statement to us in the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps. We also met him and he provided the statement, not only to me. It was not an exclusive statement, but it was provided at a press conference not far from Gorazde, and if I remember it well, it was in the spring of 1994. And I may have met him on several other occasions, which I can't really remember too well, and I don't even remember the -- why I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you must have been taking notes during the time that you had a chance to question him. A journalist always has a notebook.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: My notebook weighed 12 kilos, unfortunately, and its name was a camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you never took any written notes in your chance to ask General Gvero questions?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: If I have a 12-kilos-weighing camera on my shoulder, it is absolutely impossible to me to make any notes. So what I'm saying is you can't run your camera and make notes, so the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we see that information went out over the wires as you've acknowledged, short bits of information. Are you suggesting that that information had to be pulled from the hours of videotape that associated your various contacts with people?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not ours. Professionals working in agencies know that there are limitations on time and space, so they have to be as efficient as possible. These materials were rarely longer than 10 or 15 minutes, and you will allow me to say that it wasn't really difficult to listen to maybe 10 or 15 minutes of material because a camera will record both the image and the sound at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've never -- perhaps you can explain to me. 10 or 15 minutes, I've never seen any clips from Bosnia that were that short a time frame. They're always -- the ones -- every one I've seen, from the BBC, from Sirina [phoen], from various people, are in the hours of length, but I won't argue with you on that. Certainly, you would have some videotape of your contacts while you were in the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps prior -- about the time that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I worked in an agency. I was not a broadcaster. Agency news is short, a minute and a half to three minutes max, and that's the main and the most important difference between agency news and broadcasting news. Broadcasters use agency news; that's the reason behind the existence of agencies. All the footages that were taken anywhere or at any time in -- during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina are the property of Reuters television, and they exist among their documents. I'm sure that you can approach them with your request to get access to them, and then you can listen to the clips and watch them yourselves if they will allow you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you shooting film in this area where you were, the forward command post on July 11th, where you say you were when Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not shooting any films. What I did was making short news stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was your camera turned on? What were you making news stories of if your camera wasn't on, and how were you doing it? I thought you said your notebook was your camera.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid I would have to run a course for you on the functioning of the agencies and on the way camera crews collect information, but that's not why I was invited to come here. But, sir, you have to understand that television news stories last from a minute and a half to three minutes tops. They can be edited; they can be non-edited. And if they are raw, if they are not edited, then they are call camera piece. Whenever we go and film out in the field, we try and shoot as little material as possible, and I'm talking both about the video and audio recording, in order to waste as little time when reviewing all that material and editing it because we all in a race for time, always trying to beat our competitors. And that's why I'm asking you very kindly that if you are interested in the materials that either I or my colleagues recorded, approach the Reuters television, ask to review their documents, and then you will be able to review all that for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it was a simple question. Were you shooting any film the day Srebrenica fell, the day you have very specific recollection of meeting Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember whether on the 11th of July, 1995, I had my camera turned on and whether I recorded anything. I think so, but please allow me to have my reservations, but on the day when we heard that Srebrenica had fallen, my main preoccupation was to leave the area, go somewhere else in order to redirect my main focus on a different location, the location which at that time was interesting from the media point of view, that had a story at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long had you been at this IKM before you left to go back to Belgrade on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, this was from the morning hours until late afternoon. The sun was already falling, if I'm not mistaken, when I left that particular place but not the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long were you in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps prior to leaving on the 11th to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I left for Belgrade on the 11th, did I? On the following day or maybe I stayed even two days. I can't really tell you. I was waiting for my transportation for Belgrade to be organised, and that took time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's try to clear that up. How many days after you heard on the radio that Srebrenica fell did you go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: A day or two, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you for a fact. I can only tell you that it took a whole day or -- actually, it took up to 12 hours to get from that place to Belgrade under the conditions that prevailed at the time. That's the only thing I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you can't be sure you saw Colonel Beara, either. It might have been another VRS officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of the question, and there's no foundation for that. I don't know how he is making that connection. I think it's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is cross-examination on an alibi witness, for God's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just state for the record, and I don't mind the comments, but first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Slow, slow, slow, slow. Let's keep it cool.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I haven't said anything. I think the comments are coming from the other side. First of all, if we look at the evidence the Prosecution led, it's quite clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we do this outside the presence of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I said slow because [indiscernible] have understood me. I think you've put your argument clear enough. He has, as well. I don't think we need to hear anything else. We'll just decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a perfectly correct question. Go ahead, Mr. Grulovic. Please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood the question correctly -- or could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being put to you that perhaps you could be wrong when you say that you spoke to Beara; you could have seen some other VRS officer. If I didn't put the question correctly to the witness, Mr. McCloskey, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That will work, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I claim that I saw Colonel Beara. There is an anecdote that is tied to that encounter with him, and if you want me to do that, I can share that particular thing with you, that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you shared it with Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The anecdote.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, it's not an anecdote. It's a very dangerous thing, something that almost cost me my life, so I really wouldn't call it an anecdote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe it's a translation issue. Your answer was that there's an anecdote that would help explain the story, and I asked you if you had told that anecdote to Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Bad translation. I never said anecdote, and no, I did not share that with Mr. Ostojic. He didn't ask me. He was not in a position to ask me because he didn't know anything about that. I never told him, but I can share it with you now if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and be very concise. On that day, there was a meeting, which was attended by Colonel Beara, General Gvero, and if my memory serves me well, General Milovanovic, as well, and some other people whose names I don't know. I and another colleague of mine were in front of the building where the meeting was taking place, and close to the end of the meeting two men in uniform approached me and my colleague, and they threatened us. They told us they would be killed because we were there without any permission, that we were not authorised to be there and that we were conveying stories to the world that were not to their liking. I called General Gvero in a panic. General Gvero was just walking to his car at that moment. Colonel Beara turned up at that moment, approached these two men in a very -- in a very authoritative way. He prevented these two from inflicting physical harm on myself and my colleague. Thus, I did not want to go into any detail of the danger of that situation, but that's how I remember so well that I saw both General Gvero and Colonel Beara on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what kind of car did Gvero have?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: A passenger car, but I can't remember which make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when did you first start recalling these events, the events you've just talked about, the passenger car, Gvero, Beara, this dangerous situation you were in over 13 years ago? When did you first start recollecting these events, or perhaps you had written about them as a journalist might.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Let me start with last things first. I never wrote about this incident, and if your life is ever threatened, this is not something that takes time to recall. This is something that is deeply imbranded [sic] in your memory all your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So just right now, 13 years after the fact, you remember Gvero was with you there?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I repeat for the last or umpteenth time, yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another topic. You've talked about Colonel Beara and that you had a favourable viewpoint of him. He was nice to his mother. Would you be disappointed to learn that he used derogatory terms towards Muslim in official military documents?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a simple question. If you learned that he had repeatedly referred to Muslims as "balija" in official military documents, would you be disappointed that he would stoop to that level?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the word "balija" was in general use. It was used very often. I don't even know what the meaning of that is, and I suppose that a Bosniak, would find this derogatory. But the same goes for the word "Chetnik" when that word is used for Serbs in a negative sense, and the word is still being used. So when it comes to those local terms, I don't know. For example, this is like if I told you that we call our people who hail from Krusevac, which a town in Serbia, "carapani," this is something that is lost in translation, and you wouldn't be able to understand it. So if you were to explain to me the term "balija," what it means, maybe I would be able to answer your question whether I would be disappointed our not. Since I don't know, it's very hard for me to answer and to tell you whether I'd be disappointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you don't know what "balija" means?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't know how the word "balija" is commonly used in the Serbo-Croat language?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I know that it is used, but I don't know its meanings. I know it is applied to members of the Bosniak nation, but I don't know its meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it a -- what kind of term is it? Is it a nice term? Is it a derogatory term? Is it a neutral term?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: I would have to go into the etymology of the word, and I'm not a linguistic expert. I suppose that its origin is in the Turkish language. I repeat, I don't know. I don't know whether it's good or bad, but where I come from, different terms are used. If you were to translate our family names, you would understand how rude they may be. I can even give you examples for that, so I really wouldn't be able to give you the meaning of the word "balija." Having said that, I know that it is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go to a document, 65 ter 3510. It will come up on your board. This is a document dated 10 of April, 1995, from the VRS Main Staff, and I would note to the Court, there was a similar document in court dated 29 April, 65 ter 3497, and it was in the name of Vujadin Popovic. This one comes under the name of Colonel Ljubisa Beara and is dated a few days earlier on the 10th of April, and it's to the security department of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, the eastern -- all the corps, basically, and to the security organs of several other units. And it starts out -- and we can look at the back of it. Look at the bottom. You can see this is from Chief Colonel Ljubisa Beara. And sir, "colonel" is not here because he used the term "balija," just to make that clear, but I just want to ask you about this. The Drina corps security organs have intelligence that certain balija, Omerovic Saban, from Zutica village, Srebrenica enclave, and it goes on. I won't read it all out, but there are five references to this term "balija." Now, I received a note from Mr. Ostojic that you would be talking about the non-discriminatory mental disposition towards ethnic group, especially Muslims. If this document is genuine and Colonel Beara is five times referring to Muslims and a particular Muslim as balija, can you really testify that he doesn't have any discrimination in him?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: If this is a facsimile of the original document, the one that I have here in front of me, I can't see the signature of Colonel Beara; and let me note once again, I don't know what the word "balija" means. Could you please explain it to me, and then I'll be able to answer it once that I've learned what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll give you an example how I've heard it the most when I listen to Muslims testify or I hear their statements. It's usually coming from soldiers while Muslims are in the area, and it's usually -- they usually say something like "fuck your balija mother." Certainly you've heard that particular phrase?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what you said in our language, in our parlance, it's like, good day to you. That's how we greet each other. We say hey, hello, where are you, and then [no interpretation] your mother. So I really can't understand your question, but I say it again, if this is a facsimile of the original document, then Beara has not signed it. There's no Beara signature here, so please don't keep putting those documents in front of my nose, and I would like to ask the Trial Chamber if we could perhaps have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you. --- Break taken at 12.17 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Grulovic, are you all right now? Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, I think we'll leave that term alone and go on to something else, and if we could have 65 ter number 480 brought on the screen. But let me ask you about another ethnic term. What does the term "Siptar" refer to? It's not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what "Siptar" has to do with Bosnia, but let me tell you, "Siptar" in the Serbian language comes from the Albanian term, "soperia" [phoen] or "sopar." [phoen] I don't know if I pronounce it correctly, but it means "Albanian."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it a derogatory term for Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Recently it has come to be derogatory, but earlier it was not derogatory at all. I can say that with full authority because I spent a lot of time in Kosovo, both in business and privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know a journalist from Belgrade named Stradoja Simic, a publication called Svedok, I think.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: No. And I don't read this paper. If my mind, it's a tabloid paper, and I don't -- I've never even taken it into my hands at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I -- if we could go to page 2 in the B/C/S. We have heard from Mr. Simic who said that Colonel Beara had granted an interview and they did an interview together and that that was published in this paper, and Mr. Simic said that what was published here is accurate and -- sorry, I don't have a good B/C/S copy. It's tiny. See if I can get you a bigger one. They have blown it up a bit for you so you can see that. If we can just go -- I don't really need you to go through the whole article, but if you could just help him go through the first part of it. I really want to ask him about a question that is on page 3 of the B/C/S, page 8 of the English. I'm sorry, page 3 in the B/C/S, page 7 in the English. But if you could go down with him so he can get a bit of the flavour of this question-and-answer session. Let us know when you are finished reading, so ...

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read the first page where there is this big picture. I am sorry, it's not -- I don't have the whole one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next page or the next part so he can read the whole thing, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, let me start with page 2 in the B/C/S. That's where this term "Siptar" is used in an answer. It's page 5 in the English, and so the questioner says, "So you don't feel guilty?" If you can make that tiny print. Sorry I didn't get you a bigger print. But it begins with the question "So you don't feel guilty," and according to this article, Ljubisa Beara says, "I haven't seen the indictment yet."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please be moved up a little bit for interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "I am guilty, I suppose, just because I am a Serb. According to The Hague and those who finance the Tribunal, only the Serbs committed crimes. The Croats, Muslims, and hordes of mercenaries from all over the world are not. Only we are the aggressors and to be blamed for the civil war. Why don't they tell the truth? That Croatia organised an illegal army in the SFRY, that the Slovenes organised an armed uprising, that the patriotic league in the BH secretly organised the Green Berets, that the Siptars in Kosmet set up the OBK before the eyes of the entire world. No one wants to say that Yugoslavia was destroyed by the powerful Clinton and Solana, the peacemaker. We are just small fry, and they can do whatever they like. Who armed the Croats? Germans and the Vatican. Even the birds on the trees know that. Everyone knows it, but they are all playing the fools. They have only one objective, to put the Serbs in the ghetto." This answer suggesting all these other ethnic groups are -- but mainly I want to ask you about this idea that the Serbs are being set up, that the Serbs are being put in the ghetto, that they are the victims of everything. Do you -- what is your view of that kind of propaganda, if I may say? Unless you don't think it's propaganda.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: My personal opinion of the propaganda in this article, well, I don't see why it would be relevant because I've already said when I didn't know that you would be asking me this that I consider Svedok to be the kind of newspaper that builds its credibility and its niche on the market through sensationalism, which is contrary to professionalism. Of course, as a citizen I have my political views and opinions of what happened, and I believe that it was propaganda on all sides that did a good part of the work and that people started hating each other. Unrelated to this text, if you allow me I can give you an example of what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we would probably agree with you that propaganda played a big role in this, but I don't think we need to get into that, sir. In fact, I thank you for your time, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination? One moment. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm seeking the permission of the Court to re-examine this witness because the Prosecution devoted a good part of the cross-examination to my client, Mr. Gvero. I did not mention him at all. I could not assume that the Prosecution would be asking questions about my clients, and this has to do with the questions asked in the cross-examination by the Prosecution. I would like to ask him about the meetings with General Gvero and about how the witness saw the role and what they talked about at those meetings. General Gvero and the witness, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would object to questions relating to General Gvero's role. The article regarding General Gvero's role was on our list, and they could have questioned him on that. They did, in fact, question him on other things. However, the part where Gvero appeared with Beara is something new to everyone, and I do not object if he wishes to go into that because that is new. The other stuff is not new. Those documents, those issues were all there for one that wishes to take the risk of bringing them up. They chose not to take that risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also know what our position is when it comes to cross-examinations and not redirect, so one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Again, not to be interpreted as setting a precedent for later, we are allowing you to ask the witness questions only in relation to the last issue mentioned by Mr. McCloskey to wit the meeting with Gvero and Beara and nothing else beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, you mentioned in your response to the Prosecution that in July 1995, I think it was in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina corps that you met a number of people, including General Gvero. Do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the microphones in the courtroom please be switched off if they are not in use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you spoke with General Gvero, what was the primary concern of General Gvero? What part of the theatre, what did you talk about at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR GRULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise if my previous answer was not clear enough. I said that I was in front of the building where the meeting was taking place and that I merely said "hello" to General Gvero who was heading to his car when two persons tried to endanger my safety. I think I mentioned that Colonel Beara appeared at that time, and he responded, and the general also turned around and -- in response to my mild scream asking for help. So at that time we did not talk about anything, about any events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Republika Srpska, in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps. When this whole circus, if I may call it that, ended, General Gvero hurried away. Of course, it never occurred to me to ask him where he was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Grulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Grulovic, your testimony ends here. We don't have any further questions for you, which means that you will be assisted by our staff to return home. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and on behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The only one we used was 2D547, and we would just -- I don't know that it's necessary, but if the Court wishes it, we would offer it, but we are not insisting on that document. 2D547.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, I mean, I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then we'll tender it, Your Honour. I'm sorry. We'll tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- we should say whether we need it or not. We'll never know. Yes, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would take it that it means only that page. You are tendering only that particular page or the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The first page and the -- I think it was page 14 I think would be adequate enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objections from the other Defence teams? None. They are so admitted. Mr. Krgovic, you don't have any documents, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. 65 ter 3510, 3538, 3539, and 3540.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't think 3540 was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's Sonja's intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any objections to the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you verified, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll accept it. It just doesn't appear on WordWheel until it was mentioned just now, but it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He gave the wrong number. He gave the wrong number earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that document is also admitted. Shall we move to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Jevdevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm the presiding judge, and I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal. You have been summoned as a witness by the Defence team for the Ljubisa Beara, but before you start giving evidence you are required to undertake that you will be testifying the truth. The solemn declaration is going to be handed to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Who will be -- Mr. Nikolic from the Beara Defence team will be putting some questions to you. It will then be followed by others. We won't finish today with you, but hopefully we will be finished tomorrow. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jevdevic. As you know, my name is Predrag Nikolic, and I am part of Ljubisa Beara's Defence team. Before I start asking you questions, I would like to give you some useful advice that we both must comply with in order to enable everyone to follow our conversation. Since we both speak Serbian, we always have to make a small pause between question and answer in order to give interpreters the time to interpret everything that we've said. Can we begin now?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... also, he is not only the witness of the Beara Defence team but also of the Miletic defence team, for the record. Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself, give us your name, father's name, the place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Marinko Jevdevic. My father's name is Nedjel. I was born in Rogatica in 1968. That's where I graduated from high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your educational background, then?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the technical transport school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about your professional background after graduation?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: After graduation, I applied with the Yugoslav army to become a professional serviceman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was that? When were you a professional member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: I applied in 1991, actually, towards the end of 1991, and I started working on the 15th of March, 1992, as a member of the Uzice corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You are saying that you were a professional soldier. What was your professional duty?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: During my compulsory military service, I became a soldier specializing in anti-terrorism, and I applied to become a professional serviceman in Belgrade with this specialty, and with that specialty I was given a position in the Uzice corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay with the JNA, to be more precise, the Uzice corps?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: I stayed with the Uzice corps until 29 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: After that date, I transferred to the Army of Republika Srpska. I was supposed to report to the command at Han Pijesak where the J -- the Republika Srpska army had its barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the protection regiment, and I went to Similjajka [phoen]. That's where the protection regiment was, and I was assigned to the police company unit for anti-terrorist activity, and I was a detachment commander or a platoon commander, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Zoran Malinic, who was the battalion commander, because my company was under strength of the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the protection regiment?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: It was General Milomir Savcic, who was on sick leave at the time after having been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where was the headquarters or the base of the military police unit that you belonged to, in which part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: It was in Similjajka. We had our tents or camp there in the vicinity of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And did you stay there all the time, or did you change positions? Did you change your base?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: The military police battalion changed its base in the month of August 1993. We were relocated to Nova Kasaba. The whole battalion was relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly explain what the main tasks and duties of the military police were? I.e., what were your duties as a military policeman and the tasks that you had?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: The duties had to do with the implementation of peace and order in the military. We provided security for facilities and people. We provided security for the command post. Those were by and large our tasks, and we were also involved in the prevention of the infiltration of some groups that tried to infiltrate our territory, scar the terrain, and we also participated in some of the actions that were taking place in our parts of the battle field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you also provide security for the Main Staff and its base, its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some battalion companies did provide security for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevdevic, I'm going to show you a document now. 2D233 is its number. We also have a draft version of the English translation, which I'll kindly ask the usher to distribute among the Bench and our learned friends from the Prosecution. I apologise, the number is wrong. 2D529. 2D529. Could you please spend a moment reading this document, and when you are ready to answer my questions, give me a sign. Could the document please be blown up on the screen. The letters are too small. Now this is much better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So we can proceed. Can you tell me who issued this document? What is it about?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: It was issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the administration for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the date?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: The date is 19 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is the Main Staff talking about? Who are they informing, and what tasks are given by the Main Staff and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: What is contained in this document is information to all the corps about issues with paramilitary units that should be put under our control. This is exactly what we did in the course of 1993. This was part of our policing duty, preventing paramilitary informations, their arrest, and placing them under the control of the Army Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Please did you and who from receive tasks in relation to this document which speaks about the prevention of the paramilitary activities?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: I participated in a task which concerned the prevention of the activities of the paramilitary formations in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps; to be more precise, in Bratunac. We were given a task. I personally was given this task from Major Malinic. I was supposed to take some of my troops in an APC and go towards Bratunac where there was a group which was creating problems in the brigade. On its strength, there were some soldiers who were not actually soldiers but members of a paramilitary organisation. They belonged to some other organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you say paramilitary, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Paramilitaries are a unit that is under nobody's command or is not on the strength of the Republika Srpska army. Independent, acting independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that this was in Bratunac. Can you please tell me when it was? What year were you given that task, and what paramilitary units were in question?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: This was in spring 1992, and I can't give you the exact date when we were given our brief. When we arrived in Bratunac, we were given the brief from Major Malinic. He already had intelligence about the existence of some units or parts thereof or even some individuals who were there who were supposed to be brought in. We were even issued with the search warrants for their houses and the confiscation of their personal effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Slow down just a little. We'll come to that. I suppose that when you were given this brief that these paramilitary units and individuals had already been located, and you knew exactly where to go to carry out your order. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, if you remember, which groups were those, and how did you know that those were paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: We were given the names of three individuals. One was Bosko Crveni, Red Bosko. Red was his nickname. I don't know his family name. The other person was Bato Kocar, and the third person was a certain Kokara, whose first name I don't know, and Kokara is probably his nickname. As for Bosko Crveni, we knew at the time that he was somewhere in Erdut and that he would come to Bratunac only from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just for clarification, where is Erdut?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Erdut is somewhere in Slavonia thereabouts. I can't be sure exactly where.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is it in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in another republic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: In another republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: These individuals that you've just mentioned, were they members of the Republika Srpska army or were they acting independently together with some other groups?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: At the time they acted independently, and that's why we had been sent into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm now going to ask you to describe how you accomplished your mission. How did you proceed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime late in the afternoon or in the evening, we were told to search the family houses of the aforementioned persons. We acted in three different groups in cooperation with the military police of the Bratunac Brigades. I personally went to search Kokara's family house. We searched the premises, and we found a lot of ammunition, weaponry, and military equipment that we confiscated pursuant to the order we had to search the premises and confiscate the things that we found. We also had an order to arrest him, but we did not find him at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. How were you assisted by the Bratunac military police or the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: They went with us. They compiled the record on the procedure as well as the record of all the confiscated things, which means that everything that was confiscated was recorded by them. We were there to carry out the mission in the appropriate way, and they made the record of everything that had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you search the houses of all the three individuals that you mentioned that same evening?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we were split into three groups that worked simultaneously, and I went with one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there any incidents that evening?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: There were no incidents whatsoever. Nothing happened that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And later on, what happened? Were there any new problems? How did the individuals whose weapons had been confiscated react?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: The following day -- or rather, we were billeted in the ceramics factory in Bratunac before we were sent out on the mission. On the following day, the group appeared minus Bosko Crveni, who wasn't there. They appeared with their fellow like-minded colleagues. They turned up in our parking lot in front of the premises where we were billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that two out of the three turned up with a bigger group of the like-minded colleagues and turned up in front of the temporary headquarters of the military police in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And what happened? What was the occasion? How come they turned up?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: They turned up armed, and they circled the entire parking lot. They even provided physical security for the APC that belonged to us. They encircled that, as well, and they wanted to talk to somebody. They wanted to know who had sent us, with what authority we had done what we did. I knew Bato Kocar personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What did they want from you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to talk to one of our superiors or whoever had given us the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How did you resolve this situation?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: I spoke mostly with Bato Kocar, who was a member of the Bratunac Brigade, I believe. But at that particular time, he was not on the best of terms with the rest of the brigade. Basically, I tried to calm things down. I told him that I would inform somebody, then that very soon somebody would come to talk to him. Since we knew each other from before, we did not use force. We could deal with the matter in peaceful terms, and that's when I informed Major Malinic who had left and gone to Nova Kasaba where our command was. Major Malinic answered that he would be with us really quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And did Major Malinic really arrive soon, and what was your opinion of that in relation to the persons that came with the weapons and for all intents and purposes rebelled against a unit such as your one?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to prevent any conflict between myself and the other persons. I made the APC move away from the site, and I talked to them, and after awhile, after about half an hour, Colonel Beara wanted to talk to me using communications equipment. He asked me where Malinic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain, why did Colonel Beara want to talk to you when you informed your superior?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Beara probably went to see Malinic, and he was probably heading down towards the Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road. He probably saw Malinic, and he probably knew that I had informed Malinic about this incident, about what was going on, that they were looking for somebody to talk to about their problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you consider it logical that somebody from the security organ would want to talk to you? Was that your joint task, yours and theirs?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was quite logical to me that this was our joint task because we were also under the intelligence and security administration, and it was quite logical for Colonel Beara to send Major Malinic to deal with this, to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And what agreement did you reach with Colonel Beara regarding how to solve this whole incident?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he spoke to me very briefly using the communications equipment. He asked me, Kid, what is going on down there? And I said, Well, there's a couple of people here, somebody should talk to them. And he instructed me very briefly, telling me, Send them down there to a cafe. I think its name was Cezar or some other name. I can't really remember. I'll be down there myself, but don't tell them who is coming. And our conversation ended with that. So I went out and I told Bato Kocar and his pals that somebody would come and talk to them, and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please, in your answer you said that Colonel Beara told you, Kid, what is going on there. This form of address, does that mean that you had known each other from before?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did meet on a couple of occasions because we both belonged to the Main Staff and we were moving around that area, so we knew each other, or rather, I knew Colonel Beara from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well. Who did go to this cafe to talk to the two people or no matter how many there were? Did the escorts go there too?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. About seven or eight of them went down to that cafe, and they were waiting for somebody. I told them to just sit there and wait for awhile because somebody would be there shortly to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Fine. And please tell me, once they were gathered in this place, did you accompany Colonel Beara, and can you describe the course of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Beara arrived shortly. I got into a vehicle together with him, and we drove down to this place where they were. We entered the cafe. They were all in there sitting around the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And did the problem finally emerge? What did they ask from you and from Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: They wanted an explanation for our involvement down there, the way in which we did it. Well, they were talking about some other things, too, but I didn't linger there for a long time, so I can't really remember the course of the conversation all that well. All I know is that they were surprised when they saw him come. At that time, I got a call from Malinic over the communications equipment, and I had to go up there and fetch Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Why do you think that they were surprised when they saw Colonel Beara arrive?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably knew Colonel Beara. They knew that he was from the intelligence security administration. They didn't expect to see him, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you left that room and you went to your superior officer Malinic. Do you know how this conversation ended, and how was this whole problem involving this group of paramilitary units solved?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: I went out of the cafe to fetch Major Malinic, and I brought him back to the room where Colonel Beara was talking to those men. Malinic was present during that conversation, but soon after about an hour he called me and said that I and my soldiers should leave Bratunac and go back to our original unit, to Kasaba, in other words. He simply said, Your task is done. All the other actions that followed after that were carried out by the military police from Bratunac, from the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, you said that you had confiscated this huge pile of weapons and that you took it with you. Did this remain with the military police, or was it ever returned to those persons?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: It remained with the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, all the weapons and all the equipment, and they kept a record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: After that, were there any new problems with those persons regarding what they did, failure to obey orders, and to place themselves under the command of the regular units of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO JEVDEVIC
utterances.text: Well, after talking to Major Malinic on his return to Nova Kasaba, he said that he had -- that they had placed themselves under the command of the Republika Srpska army and that the problem was for the most part solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have now dealt with one topic, so perhaps we might finish now, and then I can launch on a new topic tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine with us. Tomorrow we sit at 9 o'clock in the morning, and we stand adjourned. Thank you. In the meantime, before -- wait one moment. One moment. Mr. Jevdevic, our rules require that since you are not finishing your testimony today, you will be continuing tomorrow, that between today and tomorrow you do not communicate with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony. You shouldn't allow anyone to approach you, and you shouldn't approach anyone to discuss the topics you are testifying about. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
